The '''Bengal tiger''' is a [[population]] of the ''[[Panthera tigris tigris]]'' subspecies and the nominate Tiger subspecies.<ref name=catsg>{{Cite journal |author1=Kitchener, A. C. |author2=Breitenmoser-Würsten, C. |author3=Eizirik, E. |author4=Gentry, A. |author5=Werdelin, L. |author6=Wilting, A. |author7=Yamaguchi, N. |author8=Abramov, A. V. |author9=Christiansen, P. |author10=Driscoll, C. |author11=Duckworth, J. W. |author12=Johnson, W. |author13=Luo, S.-J. |author14=Meijaard, E. |author15=O'Donoghue, P. |author16=Sanderson, J. |author17=Seymour, K. |author18=Bruford, M. |author19=Groves, C. |author20=Hoffmann, M. |author21=Nowell, K. |author22=Timmons, Z. |author23=Tobe, S. |name-list-style=amp |year=2017 |title=A revised taxonomy of the Felidae: The final report of the Cat Classification Task Force of the IUCN Cat Specialist Group |journal=Cat News |issue=Special Issue 11 |pages=66–68 |url=https://repository.si.edu/bitstream/handle/10088/32616/A_revised_Felidae_Taxonomy_CatNews.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y}}</ref> It ranks among the biggest wild cats alive today.<ref name=Mazak1981>{{Cite journal |author=Mazák, V. |year=1981 |title=''Panthera tigris'' |journal=Mammalian Species |issue=152 |pages=1–8 |doi=10.2307/3504004 |jstor=3504004 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Geptner1972">{{Cite book |author1=Heptner, V. G. |author2=Sludskij, A. A. |name-list-style=amp |orig-year=1972 |year=1992 |title=Mlekopitajuščie Sovetskogo Soiuza. Moskva: Vysšaia Škola |trans-title=Mammals of the Soviet Union. Volume II, Part 2. Carnivora (Hyaenas and Cats) |publisher=Smithsonian Institution and the National Science Foundation |location=Washington DC |chapter=Tiger |chapter-url=https://archive.org/stream/mammalsofsov221992gept#page/94/mode/2up |pages=95–202}}</ref> It is considered to belong to the world's [[charismatic megafauna]].<ref name="Sankhala1978">{{Cite book |last1=Sankhala |first1=K. |author-link=Kailash Sankhala |title=Tiger: The Story of the Indian Tiger |date=1978 |publisher=Collins |isbn=978-0002161244 |location=Glasgow}}</ref>

The tiger is estimated to have been present in the [[Indian subcontinent]] since the [[Late Pleistocene]], for about 12,000 to 16,500 years.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kitchener |first1=A. C. |last2=Dugmore |first2=A. J. |name-list-style=amp |year=2000 |title=Biogeographical change in the tiger, ''Panthera tigris'' |journal=Animal Conservation |volume=3 |issue=2 |pages=113–124 |doi=10.1111/j.1469-1795.2000.tb00236.x |s2cid=86096562 }}</ref><ref name="Luo2004">{{Cite journal |last1=Luo |first1=S. J. |last2=Kim |first2=J. |last3=Johnson |first3=W. E. |last4=van der Walt |first4=J. |last5=Martenson |first5=J. |last6=Yuhki |first6=N. |last7=Miquelle |first7=D. G. |last8=Uphyrkina |first8=O. |last9=Goodrich |first9=J. M. |last10=Quigley |first10=H. B. |last11=Tilson |first11=R. |last12=Brady |first12=G. |last13=Martelli |first13=P. |last14=Subramaniam |first14=V. |last15=McDougal |first15=C. |last16=Hean |first16=S. |last17=Huang |first17=S. |last18=Pan |first18=W. |last19=Karanth |first19=U. |last20=Sunquist |first20=M. |last21=Smith |first21=J. L. D. |last22=O'Brien |first22=S. J. |name-list-style=amp |year=2004 |title=Phylogeography and Genetic Ancestry of Tigers (''Panthera tigris'') |journal=PLOS Biology |volume=2 |issue=12 |pages=e442 |doi=10.1371/journal.pbio.0020442 |pmid=15583716 |pmc=534810}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cooper |first1=D. M. |last2=Dugmore |first2=A. J. |last3=Gittings |first3=B. M. |last4=Scharf |first4=A. K. |last5=Wilting |first5=A. |last6=Kitchener |first6=A. C. |name-list-style=amp |year=2016 |title=Predicted Pleistocene–Holocene rangeshifts of the tiger (''Panthera tigris'') |journal=Diversity and Distributions |volume=22 |issue=11 |pages=1–13 |doi=10.1111/ddi.12484 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Today, it is threatened by [[poaching]], [[Habitat loss|loss]] and [[Habitat fragmentation|fragmentation]] of habitat, and was estimated at comprising fewer than 2,500 wild individuals by 2011. None of the ''Tiger Conservation Landscapes'' within its range is considered large enough to support an effective population of more than 250 adult individuals.<ref name=iucn>{{Cite iucn |title=''Panthera tigris'' |name-list-style=amp |author1=Goodrich, J. |author2=Lynam, A. |author3=Miquelle, D. |author4=Wibisono, H. |author5=Kawanishi, K. |author6=Pattanavibool, A. |author7=Htun, S. |author8=Tempa, T. |author9=Karki, J. |author10=Jhala, Y. |author11=Karanth, U. |page=e.T15955A50659951 |date=2015}}</ref>

The Bengal tiger's historical range covered the [[Indus River]] valley until the early 19th century, almost all of [[India]], [[Pakistan]], southern [[Nepal]], [[Bangladesh]], [[Bhutan]] and southwestern [[China]]. Today, it inhabits India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan and southwestern China.<ref name="Luo2004"/> India's tiger population was estimated at 2,603–3,346 individuals by 2018.<ref name=Jhala2019>{{Cite report |author=Jhala, Y.V. |author-link=Yadvendradev Vikramsinh Jhala |author2=Qureshi, Q. |author3=Nayak, A.K. |name-list-style=amp |year=2020 |title=Status of tigers, co-predators and prey in India 2018 |publisher=National Tiger Conservation Authority, Government of India, Wildlife Institute of India |location=New Delhi, Dehradun |url=http://moef.gov.in/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Tiger-Status-Report-2018_For-Web_compressed_compressed.pdf}}</ref>
Around 300–500 individuals are estimated in Bangladesh,<ref name=iucn/> 355 in Nepal by 2022,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://edition.cnn.com/2022/07/31/world/nepal-wild-tiger-population-scn-trnd/index.html|title=Nepal has nearly tripled its wild tiger population since 2009|last=Sottile|first=Zoe|date=31 July 2022|publisher=[[CNN]]|access-date=1 August 2022}}</ref> and 90 individuals in Bhutan by 2015.<ref name=Tempa_al2019/>

==Taxonomy==
''Felis tigris'' was the [[scientific name]] used by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1758 for the tiger.<ref name="Linn1758">{{Cite book |author=Linnaeus, C. |year=1758 |title=Caroli Linnæi Systema naturæ per regna tria naturæ, secundum classes, ordines, genera, species, cum characteribus, differentiis, synonymis, locis. Tomus I |edition=decima, reformata |location=Holmiae |publisher=Laurentius Salvius |chapter=''Felis tigris'' |page=41 |chapter-url=https://archive.org/stream/mobot31753000798865#page/41/mode/2up}}</ref> It was subordinated to the [[genus]] ''Panthera'' by [[Reginald Innes Pocock]] in 1929. [[Bengal]] is the traditional [[Type (biology)|type]] locality of the species and the [[nominate subspecies]] ''Panthera tigris tigris''.<ref name=Pocock1929>{{Cite journal |author=Pocock, R. I. |year=1929 |title=Tigers |journal=Journal of the Bombay Natural History Society |volume=33 |issue=3 |pages=505–541 |url=https://archive.org/details/journalofbomb33341929bomb/page/n133}}</ref>

The [[Valid name (zoology)|validity]] of several tiger subspecies in continental Asia was questioned in 1999. [[Morphology (biology)|Morphologically]], tigers from different regions vary little, and [[gene flow]] between populations in those regions is considered to have been possible during the [[Pleistocene]]. Therefore, it was proposed to recognise only two subspecies as valid, namely ''P. t. tigris'' in mainland Asia, and [[Javan tiger|''P. t. sondaica'']] in the [[Greater Sunda Islands]] and possibly in [[Sundaland]].<ref name="Kitchener1999">{{Cite book |last=Kitchener |first=A. |title=Riding the Tiger: Tiger Conservation in Human-Dominated Landscapes |date=1999 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-64835-6 |editor1-last=Seidensticker |editor1-first=J. |pages=19–39 |chapter=Tiger distribution, phenotypic variation and conservation issues |editor2-last=Christie |editor2-first=S. |editor3-last=Jackson |editor3-first=P. |chapter-url=http://www.nfwf.org/AM/Template.cfm?Section=Home&CONTENTID=3060&TEMPLATE=/CM/ContentDisplay.cfm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120423162028/http://www.nfwf.org/AM/Template.cfm?Section=Home |archive-date=23 April 2012 |url-status=dead}}</ref> The [[nominate subspecies]] ''P. t. tigris'' constitutes two [[clade]]s: the northern clade comprises the Siberian and Caspian tiger populations, and the southern clade all remaining continental tiger populations.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Planning tiger recovery: Understanding intraspecific variation for effective conservation |last1=Wilting |first1=A. |last2=Courtiol |first2=A. |first3=P. |last3=Christiansen |first4=J. |last4=Niedballa |first5=A. K. |last5=Scharf |first6=L. |last6=Orlando |first7=N. |last7=Balkenhol |first8=H. |last8=Hofer |first9=S.|last9=Kramer-Schadt |first10=J. |last10=Fickel |first11=A. C. |last11=Kitchener |display-authors=5 |year=2015 |volume=11 |issue=5: e1400175 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.1400175 |pmid = 26601191|pmc=4640610 |journal=Science Advances |pages=e1400175 |bibcode=2015SciA....1E0175W}}</ref> The [[extinct]] and living tiger [[population]]s in continental Asia have been subsumed to ''P. t. tigris'' since the revision of felid taxonomy in 2017.<ref name=catsg/>

Results of a genetic analysis of 32 tiger samples indicate that the Bengal tiger samples grouped into a different [[clade]] than the Siberian tiger samples.<ref name="Liu_al2018">{{Cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=Y.-C. |first2=X. |last2=Sun |first3=C. |last3=Driscoll |first4=D. G. |last4=Miquelle |first5=X. |last5=Xu |first6=P. |last6=Martelli |first7=O. |last7=Uphyrkina |first8=J. L. D. |last8=Smith |first9=S. J. |last9=O’Brien |first10=S.-J. |last10=Luo |display-authors=5 |title=Genome-wide evolutionary analysis of natural history and adaptation in the world's tigers |journal=Current Biology |volume=28 |issue=23 |year=2018 |pages=3840–3849 |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2018.09.019 |pmid=30482605|doi-access=free }}</ref>

===Genetic ancestry===
The Bengal tiger is defined by three distinct [[mitochondrial]] [[nucleotide]] sites and 12 unique [[Microsatellite (genetics)|microsatellite]] alleles. The pattern of [[genetic variation]] in the Bengal tiger corresponds to the premise that it arrived in India approximately 12,000 years ago.<ref>{{Cite journal |author=Kitchener, A. C. |author2=Dugmore, A. J. |year=2000 |title=Biogeographical change in the tiger, ''Panthera tigris''|journal= Animal Conservation |volume=3 |pages= 113–124|doi=10.1111/j.1469-1795.2000.tb00236.x|issue=2|s2cid=86096562 }}</ref> This is consistent with the lack of tiger [[fossil]]s from the Indian subcontinent prior to the late Pleistocene, and the absence of tigers from [[Sri Lanka]], which was separated from the subcontinent by [[sea level rise|rising sea levels]] in the early [[Holocene]].<ref name="Luo2004"/>

==Characteristics==
{{Multiple image |align=right |direction=vertical |image1=Tiger facial marking Sultan (T72) Ranthambhore India 12.10.2014.jpg |caption1=Facial close up of Sultan, a male in Ranthambore National Park |image2=White-tiger-2407799 1280.jpg |caption2=A white tiger}}
The Bengal tiger's coat is yellow to light orange, with stripes ranging from dark brown to black; the belly and the interior parts of the limbs are white, and the tail is orange with black rings. The [[white tiger]] is a [[recessive]] [[Mutants|mutant]], which is reported in the wild from time to time in [[Assam]], Bengal, [[Bihar]], and especially in the former [[Rewa (princely state)|State of Rewa]]. However, it is not an occurrence of [[albinism]]. In fact, there is only one fully authenticated case of a true albino tiger, and none of black tigers, with the possible exception of one dead specimen examined in [[Chittagong]] in 1846.<ref name=McDougal1977>{{Cite book |last=McDougal |first=C. |year=1977 |title=The Face of the Tiger |publisher=Rivington Books and André Deutsch |location=London}}</ref> Fourteen Bengal tiger skins in the collection of the [[Natural History Museum, London]] have 21–29 stripes.<ref name="Kitchener1999"/>
Another [[recessive]] mutant is the [[golden tiger]] that has a pale golden fur with red-brown stripes.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Xu, X. |author2=Dong, G. X. |author3=Schmidt-Küntzel, A. |author4=Zhang, X. L. |author5=Zhuang, Y. |author6=Fang, R. |author7=Sun, X. |author8=Hu, X.S. |author9=Zhang, T. Y. |author10=Yang, H. D. |author11=Zhang, D. L. |author12=Marker, L. |author13=Jiang, Z.-F. |author14=Li, R. |author15=Luo, S.-J. |year=2017 |title=The genetics of tiger pelage color variations |journal=Cell Research |volume=27 |issue=7 |pages=954–957 |doi=10.1038/cr.2017.32 |pmid=28281538 |pmc=5518981 |url=https://www.luo-lab.org/publications/Xu17-CellRes-GoldenTiger.pdf}}</ref> The mutants are very rare in nature.<ref>{{cite web |title=Colour aberration in tiger: its biological and conservation implications. Summary of Talk at National Seminar "Tiger Tiger", 4–5 August 2000, Indian Museum, Calcutta |author=Singh, L. A. K.|date=2000 |place=Calcutta |publisher=Indian Museum |url=https://www.academia.edu/7819624/Singh_L._A._K._2000_Colour_aberration_in_tiger_its_biological_and_conservation_implications._Summary_of_Talk_at_National_Seminar_Tiger_Tiger_4-5_August_2000_Indian_Museum_Calcutta}}</ref>

The greatest skull length of a tiger is {{Cvt|351|mm}} in males and {{Cvt|293|mm}} in females.<ref>{{Cite book |author1=Kitchener, A. |name-list-style=amp |author2=Yamaguchi, N. |year=2010 |orig-year=First published 1987 |title=Tigers of the World |edition=2nd |publisher=Academic Press |editor1=Tilson, R. |editor2=Nyhus, P.J. |chapter=What is a tiger? Biogeography, Morphology, and Taxonomy |page=55 |doi=10.1016/B978-0-8155-1570-8.00004-9 |chapter-url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/266794969 |isbn=978-0-8155-1570-8}}</ref> It has exceptionally stout teeth. Its canines are {{Cvt|7.5|to|10|cm}} long and thus the longest among all cats.<ref name="S&S02">{{Cite book |last1=Sunquist |first1=M. |last2=Sunquist |first2=F. |title=Wild Cats of the World |year=2002 |publisher=University of Chicago Press |isbn=978-0-22-677999-7 |pages=343–372 |chapter=Tiger ''Panthera tigris'' (Linnaeus, 1758) |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IF8nDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA344}}</ref>

===Body weight and size===
Males and female Bengal tigers in Panna Tiger Reserve reach a head-to-body length of {{Cvt|183|-|211|cm}} and {{Cvt|164|-|193|cm}} respectively, including a tail about {{Cvt|85|-|110|cm}} long. Total length ranges from {{Cvt|283|to|311|cm}} for male tigers and {{Cvt|255|-|285|cm}} for female tigers.<ref name=BookletOnTigerBodyGrowth2021>{{Cite book |author1=Sharma, U. K. |author2=TR, V. |author3=Gupta, S. K. |date=2021 |title=Booklet on Growth Data of Physical Characteristics and Use of Tranquilization/Antidote Drugs, Induction Time, Reversal Time for Free Ranging Royal Bengal Tiger (''Panthera tigris'') |publisher=Panna Tiger Reserve |place=Panna, Madhya Pradesh |url=https://www.pannatigerreserve.in/BOOKLET%20ON%20TIGER%20BODY%20GROWTH%20.pdf}}</ref> They typically range from {{Cvt|90|-|110|cm}} in shoulder height.<ref name=Karanth03>{{Cite journal |author=Karanth, K. U. |year=2003 |title=Tiger ecology and conservation in the Indian subcontinent |journal=Journal of the Bombay Natural History Society |volume=100 |issue=2–3 |pages=169–189 |url=http://www.nfwf.org/AM/Template.cfm?Section=Home&TEMPLATE=/CM/ContentDisplay.cfm&CONTENTID=8073 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120310174120/http://www.nfwf.org/AM/Template.cfm?Section=Home&TEMPLATE=%2FCM%2FContentDisplay.cfm&CONTENTID=8073 |archive-date=10 March 2012}}</ref>

Subadult males weigh between {{Cvt|130|and|170|kg}} and reach {{Cvt|200|to|260|kg}} when adult; subadult females weigh {{Cvt|80|to|100|kg}} and reach between {{Cvt|110|and|180|kg}} when adult.<ref name=Jhala2017>{{Cite journal |author1=Sadhu, A. |author2= Jayam, P.P.C. |author3=Qureshi, Q. |author4=Shekhawat, R. S. |author5=Sharma, S. |author6=Jhala, Y. V. |name-list-style=amp |date=2017 |journal=BMC Zoology |volume=2 |issue=16 |title=Demography of a small, isolated tiger (Panthera tigris tigris) population in a semi-arid region of western India. Appendix 1: Field Guide for Ageing Tigers |doi=10.1186/s40850-017-0025-y |s2cid= 23235257 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/322963058}}</ref> In central India, 42 adult male Bengal tigers weighed on average {{Cvt|190|kg}} with a range of {{Cvt|167-234|kg}}; their total length was {{Cvt|282|cm}} with a range of {{Cvt|267–312|cm}}, and their average shoulder height was {{Cvt|99|cm}}; 39 adult female Bengal tigers weighed an average of {{Cvt|132|kg}} with a maximum of {{Cvt|156|kg}} and an average total length of {{Cvt|254|cm}} ranging from {{Cvt|239|to|277|cm}}.<ref name=Brander1923>{{Cite book |last=Brander |first=A. A. D. |date=1923 |title=Wild Animals in Central India |location=London |publisher=Edwin Arnold & Co. |url=https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.284797}}</ref>
Several scientists indicated that adult male Bengal tigers in the [[Terai]] consistently attain more than {{Cvt|227|kg}} of body weight. Seven adult males captured in [[Chitwan National Park]] in the early 1970s had an average weight of {{Cvt|235|kg}} ranging from {{Cvt|200|to|261|kg}}, and that of the females was {{Cvt|140|kg}} ranging from {{Cvt|116|to|164|kg}}.<ref>{{Cite journal |author1=Smith, J. L. D. |author2=Sunquist, M. E. |author3=Tamang, K. M. |author4=Rai, P. B. |date=1983 |title=A technique for capturing and immobilizing tigers |journal=The Journal of Wildlife Management |volume=47 |issue=1 |pages=255–259 |jstor=3808080 |doi=10.2307/3808080}}</ref> Two male tigers captured in Chitwan National Park in the 1980s exceeded weights of {{Cvt|270|kg}} and are the largest free ranging tigers reported to date.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dinerstein |first=E. |year=2003 |title=Return of the Unicorns: Natural History and Conservation of the Greater-One Horned Rhinoceros |chapter=Ecosystem Dynamics |pages=43–46 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=o6HuJQBmtksC&pg=PA44 |publisher=Columbia University Press |isbn=978-0-231-08450-5}}</ref>

The smallest recorded weights for Bengal tigers are from the Bangladesh Sundarbans, where adult females weigh {{Cvt|75|to|80|kg}}.<ref name=Barlow10>{{Cite journal |author1=Barlow, A. |author2=Mazák, J. |author3=Ahmad, I. U. |author4=Smith, J. L. D. |title=A preliminary investigation of Sundarbans tiger morphology |journal=[[Mammalia (journal)|Mammalia]] |year=2010 |volume=74 |pages=329–331 |issue=3 |doi=10.1515/mamm.2010.040|s2cid=84134909}}</ref>
Three tigresses from the Bangladesh Sundarbans had a mean weight of {{Cvt|76.7|kg}}. The oldest female weighed {{Cvt|75|kg}} and was in a relatively poor condition at the time of capture. Their skulls and body weights were distinct from those of tigers in other habitats, indicating that they may have adapted to the unique conditions of the mangrove habitat. Their small sizes are probably due to a combination of intense intraspecific competition and small size of prey available to tigers in the Sundarbans, compared to the larger deer and other prey available to tigers in other parts.<ref name=Sundarbans>{{Cite thesis |last1=Barlow |first1=A. C. D. |title=The Sundarbans Tiger – Adaptation, population status, and Conflict management |type=PhD thesis |year=2009 |url=http://www.carnivoreconservation.org/files/thesis/barlow_2009_phd.pdf |publisher=[[University of Minnesota]] |location=Minneapolis}}</ref>

The very large "[[Leeds Tiger]]" on display at [[Leeds City Museum]], shot in 1860 near [[Mussoorie]], had a body length of {{Cvt|12|ft|2|in|cm|order=flip}} at death. Two tigers shot in [[Kumaon District]] and near [[Oude]] at the end of the 19th century allegedly measured more than {{Cvt|12|ft|cm|order=flip}}. But at the time, sportsmen had not yet adopted a standard system of measurement; some measured [[wikt:peg|'between the pegs']] while others measured 'over the curves'.<ref>{{Cite book |author=Sterndale, R. A. |year=1884 |chapter-url=http://www.gutenberg.org/files/19550/19550-h/19550-h.htm#201 |chapter=''Felis Tigris'' No. 201 |title=Natural History of the Mammalia of India and Ceylon |publisher=Thacker, Spink and Co. |location=Calcutta}}</ref> The greatest length of a tiger skull measured {{Cvt|16.25|in|mm|order=flip}} "over the bone"; this one was shot in the vicinity of [[Nagina]] in northern India.<ref name=Hewett&Hewett>{{Cite book |author1=Hewett, J. P. |author2=Hewett Atkinson, L. |title=Jungle trails in northern India: reminiscences of hunting in India |publisher=Metheun and Company Limited |location=London |year=1938 |chapter=Visits to India after Retirement |pages=177–183 |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.209125/page/n225}}</ref>

In the beginning of the 20th century, a male tiger was shot in central India with a head and body length of {{Cvt|221|cm}} between pegs, a chest girth of {{Cvt|150|cm}}, a shoulder height of {{Cvt|109|cm}} and a tail length of {{Cvt|81|cm|in}}, which was perhaps bitten off by a rival male. This specimen could not be weighed, but it was estimated to weigh about {{Cvt|272|kg}}.<ref name=Brander1923/> A male weighing {{Cvt|570|lb|kg|0|order=flip}} was shot in northern India in the 1930s.<ref name="Hewett&Hewett" /> A male tiger shot in Nepal weighed {{Cvt|320|kg}} and measured {{Cvt|10|ft|9|in|cm|order=flip}} 'over the curves'.<ref>{{Cite book|author=Smythies, E. A. |title=Big game shooting in Nepal |publisher=Thacker, Spink |place=Calcutta |page=36|year=1942}}</ref>
The heaviest wild tiger was possibly a huge male killed in 1967 at the foothills of the Himalayas. It weighed {{Cvt|388.7|kg}} after eating a buffalo calf; it measured {{Cvt|323|cm}} in total length between pegs, and {{Cvt|338|cm}} over curves. Without eating the calf beforehand, it would have likely weighed at least {{Cvt|324.3|kg}}. This specimen is on exhibition in the Mammals Hall of the [[Smithsonian Institution]].<ref name=Wood1983>{{Cite book |last=Wood |first=G. L. |year=1982 |title=The Guinness Book of Animal Facts and Feats |publisher=Guinness Superlatives |location=Enfield, Middlesex |isbn=978-0-85112-235-9 |page=33}}</ref> In the Central Provinces of India, a male tiger shot weighed {{Cvt|317|kg}} and measured {{Cvt|9|ft|11|in|order=flip}}.<ref>{{Cite book|author=Ward, R. |title=Records Of Big Game |publisher=Rowland Ward, Ltd. |page=493 |year=1907 |url=https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.221504/page/n511/mode/2up}}</ref>

The Bengal tiger rivals the [[Siberian tiger]] in average weight.<ref name=Slaght2005>{{Cite book |author1=Slaght, J. C. |author2=Miquelle, D. G. |author3=Nikolaev, I. G. |author4=Goodrich, J. Who‘s king of the beasts? ==Distribution and habitat==
In 1982, a sub-[[fossil]] right middle [[Phalanx bone|phalanx]] was found in a prehistoric [[midden]] near [[Kuruwita]] in [[Sri Lanka]], which is dated to about 16,500 years ago and tentatively considered to be of a tiger. Tigers appear to have arrived in Sri Lanka during a [[pluvial]] period, during which sea levels were depressed, evidently prior to the last [[glacial maximum]] about 20,000 years ago.<ref>{{Cite journal |author1=Manamendra-Arachchi, K. |author2=Pethiyagoda, R. |author3=Dissanayake, R. |author4=Meegaskumbura, M. |year=2005 |url=http://rmbr.nus.edu.sg/rbz/biblio/s12/s12rbz423-434.pdf |title=A second extinct big cat from the late Quaternary of Sri Lanka |journal=The Raffles Bulletin of Zoology |volume=2005 |issue=Supplement No. 12 |pages=423–434 |access-date=25 April 2009 |archive-date=25 December 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181225033149/http://rmbr.nus.edu.sg/rbz/biblio/s12/s12rbz423-434.pdf%20 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The tiger probably arrived too late in southern India to colonise Sri Lanka, which earlier had been connected to India by a [[land bridge]].<ref name=Pocock1929/>

Results of a [[phylogeography|phylogeographic]] study using 134 samples from tigers across the global range suggest that the historical northeastern distribution limit of the Bengal tiger is the region in the [[Chittagong Hills]] and [[Brahmaputra River]] basin, bordering the historical range of the [[Indochinese tiger]].<ref name="Luo2004"/><ref name=Luo10>{{Cite journal |author=Luo, S.J. |author2=Johnson, W. E. |author3=O'Brien, S. J. |year=2010 |title=Applying molecular genetic tools to tiger conservation |journal=Integrative Zoology |volume=5 |issue=4 |pages=351–362|pmid=21392353 |doi=10.1111/j.1749-4877.2010.00222.x|pmc=6984346 }}</ref>
In the Indian subcontinent, tigers inhabit [[tropics|tropical]] moist [[evergreen forests]], [[tropical dry forest]]s, tropical and subtropical moist [[deciduous forest]]s, [[mangroves]], subtropical and temperate upland forests, and [[alluvial]] grasslands. The latter habitat once covered a huge swath of grassland, riverine and moist semi-deciduous forests along the major river system of the [[Gangetic plain|Gangetic]] and [[Brahmaputra River|Brahmaputra plains]], but has now been largely converted to agricultural land or severely [[Environmental degradation|degraded]]. Today, the best examples of this habitat type are limited to a few blocks at the base of the outer foothills of the [[Himalayas]] including the ''Tiger Conservation Units'' (TCUs) [[Rajaji National Park|Rajaji]]-[[Corbett National Park|Corbett]], [[Bardia National Park|Bardia]]-[[Banke National Park|Banke]], and the transboundary TCUs [[Chitwan National Park|Chitwan]]-[[Parsa National Park|Parsa]]-[[Valmiki National Park|Valmiki]], [[Dudhwa Tiger Reserve|Dudhwa]]-[[Kailali District|Kailali]] and [[Shuklaphanta National Park|Shuklaphanta]]-[[Kishanpur Wildlife Sanctuary|Kishanpur]]. Tiger densities in these TCUs are high, in part because of the extraordinary biomass of [[ungulate]] prey.<ref name="Wikramanayake1999">{{Cite book |author1=Wikramanayake, E.D. |author2=Dinerstein, E. |author3=Robinson, J.G. |author4=Karanth, K.U. |author5=Rabinowitz, A. |author6=Olson, D. |author7=Mathew, T. |author8=Hedao, P. |author9=Connor, M. |author10=Hemley, G. |author11=Bolze, D. |display-authors=5 |date=1999 |chapter=Where can tigers live in the future? A framework for identifying high-priority areas for the conservation of tigers in the wild |chapter-url=http://www.nfwf.org/AM/Template.cfm?Section=Riding_The_Tiger1&template=%2FCM%2FContentDisplay.cfm&ContentID=3062 |editor1-last=Seidensticker |editor1-first=J. |editor2-last=Christie |editor2-first=S. |editor3-last=Jackson |editor3-first=P. |title=Riding the Tiger: Tiger Conservation in Human-Dominated Landscapes |publisher=Cambridge University Press |pages=255–272 |isbn=978-0-521-64835-6 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120310110401/http://www.nfwf.org/AM/Template.cfm?Section=Riding_The_Tiger1&template=%2FCM%2FContentDisplay.cfm&ContentID=3062 |archive-date=10 March 2012 }}</ref>

Based on the result of these surveys, the total tiger population was estimated at 1,411 individuals ranging from 1,165 to 1,657 adult and sub-adult tigers of more than 1.5 years of age. Since 2007, tiger monitoring surveys have been carried out every year by [[WildTeam]] in the Bangladesh Sundarbans to monitor changes in the Bangladesh tiger population and assess the effectiveness of conservation actions. This survey measures changes in the frequency of tiger track sets along the sides of tidal waterways as an index of relative tiger abundance across the Sundarbans landscape.<ref>{{Cite journal |author=Barlow, A. |author2=Ahmed, M. By 2009, the tiger population in the Bangladesh Sundarbans was estimated as 100–150 adult females or 335–500 tigers overall. Female home ranges, recorded using [[Global Positioning System]] collars, were some of the smallest recorded for tigers, indicating that the Bangladesh Sundarbans could have one of the highest densities and largest populations of tigers anywhere in the world. They are isolated from the next tiger population by a distance of up to {{Cvt|300|km|mi}}. Information is lacking on many aspects of Sundarbans tiger ecology, including relative abundance, population status, spatial dynamics, habitat selection, life history characteristics, taxonomy, genetics, and disease. There is also no monitoring program in place to track changes in the tiger population over time, and therefore no way of measuring the response of the population to conservation activities or threats. Most studies have focused on the tiger-human conflict in the area, but two studies in the Sundarbans East Wildlife sanctuary documented habitat-use patterns of tigers, and abundances of tiger prey, and another study investigated tiger parasite load. Some major threats to tigers have been identified. The tigers living in the Sundarbans are threatened by habitat destruction, prey depletion, highly aggressive and rampant [[intraspecific competition]], tiger-human conflict, and direct tiger loss.<ref name=Sundarbans/>

==Ecology and behaviour==
{{Multiple image |align=right |direction=vertical |image1=T 17 (Panthera tigris) - Koshyk.jpg |caption1=A tigress having a bath in Ranthambore Tiger Reserve, [[Rajasthan]] |image2=India Tiger cubs.jpg |caption2=A tigress with her cubs in [[Bandhavgarh National Park]], Madhya Pradesh |image3=Flying Princess (cropped).jpg |caption3=Female cubs playing in Ranthambore Tiger Reserve}}

The basic social unit of the tiger is composed of a female and her offspring. Adult animals congregate only temporarily when special conditions permit, such as plentiful supplies of food. Otherwise, they lead solitary lives, hunting individually for the forest and grassland animals upon which they prey. Resident adults of either sex maintain home ranges, confining their movements to definite habitats within which they satisfy their needs and those of their cubs, which include prey, water and shelter. In this site, they also maintain contact with other tigers, especially those of the opposite sex. Those sharing the same ground are well aware of each other's movements and activities.<ref name="McDougal1977"/> In [[Chitwan National Park]], [[Radio telemetry|radio-collared]] subadult tigers started [[Dispersal (ecology)|dispersing]] from their natal areas earliest at the age of 19 months. Of the 14 subadults studied, the four females stayed closer to their mother's home range than the 10 males. The latter dispersed between {{Cvt|9.5|and|65.7|km}}. None of them crossed open cultivated areas that were more than {{Cvt|10|km}} wide, but moved through prime alluvial and forested habitat.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Smith |first=J. L. D. |year=1993 |title=The role of dispersal in structuring the Chitwan tiger population |volume=124 |journal=Behaviour |issue=3 |pages=165–195 |doi=10.1163/156853993X00560}}</ref>

In the Panna Tiger Reserve, an adult radio-collared male tiger moved {{Cvt|1.7|to|10.5|km}} between locations on successive days in winter, and {{Cvt|1|to|13.9|km}} in summer. His home range was about {{Cvt|200|km2}} in summer and {{Cvt|110|km2}} in winter. Included in his home range were the much smaller home ranges of two females, a tigress with cubs and a subadult tigress. They occupied home ranges of {{Cvt|16|to|31|km2}}.<ref>{{Cite book |author1=Chundawat, T. S. |author2=Gogate, N. |author3=Johnsingh, A. J. T. |date=1999 |chapter=Tigers in Panna: preliminary results from an Indian tropical dry forest |editor1-last=Seidensticker |editor1-first=J. |editor2-last=Christie |editor2-first=S. |editor3-last=Jackson |editor3-first=P. |title=Riding the Tiger: Tiger Conservation in Human-Dominated Landscapes |publisher=Cambridge University Press |pages=123–129 |isbn=978-0-521-64835-6 |chapter-url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/284088208}}</ref>

The home ranges occupied by adult male residents tend to be mutually exclusive, even though one of these residents may tolerate a transient or sub-adult male at least for a time. A male tiger keeps a large territory in order to include the home ranges of several females within its bounds, so that he may maintain [[mating]] rights with them. Spacing among females is less complete. Typically there is partial overlap with neighbouring female residents. They tend to have core areas, which are more exclusive, at least for most of the time. Home ranges of both males and females are not stable. The shift or alteration of a home range by one animal is correlated with a shift of another. Shifts from less suitable habitat to better ones are made by animals that are already resident. New animals become residents only as vacancies occur when a former resident moves out or dies. There are more places for resident females than for resident males.<ref name="McDougal1977"/>

During seven years of camera trapping, tracking, and observational data in Chitwan National Park, six to nine breeding tigers, two to sixteen non-breeding tigers, and six to twenty young tigers of less than one year of age were detected in the study area of {{Cvt|100|km2}}. One of the resident females left her territory to one of her female offspring and took over an adjoining area by displacing another female; and a displaced female managed to re-establish herself in a neighbouring territory made vacant by the death of the resident. Of 11 resident females, 7 were still alive at the end of the study period, two disappeared after losing their territories to rivals, and two died. The initial loss of two resident males and subsequent take over of their home ranges by new males caused social instability for two years. Of four resident males, one was still alive and three were displaced by rivals. Five litters of cubs were killed by infanticide, two litters died because they were too young to fend for themselves when their mothers died. One juvenile tiger was presumed dead after being photographed with severe injuries from a deer [[snare trap|snare]]. The remaining young lived long enough to reach dispersal age, two of them becoming residents in the study area.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Barlow |first1=A. C. D. |last2=McDougal |first2=C. |last3=Smith |first3=J. L. D. |last4=Gurung |first4=B. |last5=Bhatta |first5=S. R. |last6=Kumal |first6=S. |last7=Mahato |first7=B. |last8=Tamang |first8=D. ===Hunting and diet===
[[File:RANTHAMBORE TIGER RESERVE.jpg|thumb|A tiger attacking a [[Sambar deer]] in Ranthambore Tiger Reserve]]
The tiger is a [[carnivore]] and prefers hunting large [[ungulate]]s such as [[gaur]], [[Sambar (deer)|sambar]], [[chital]], [[barasingha]], [[water buffalo]], [[nilgai]], [[serow]] and [[takin]]. Medium-sized prey includes [[wild boar]], [[Indian hog deer]], [[Indian muntjac]] and [[northern plains gray langur]]. Small prey such as [[porcupine]], [[hare]] and [[peafowl]] form a small part of its diet. Because of the encroachment of humans into tiger habitat, it also preys on domestic livestock.<ref>{{Cite journal |author=Bagchi, S. |author2=Goyal, S. The prey species included chital, sambar, wild pig and gaur. Gaur remains were found in 44.8% of all tiger scat samples, sambar remains in 28.6%, wild pig remains in 14.3% and chital remains in 10.4% of all scat samples.<ref name="K&S95">{{Cite journal |last1=Karanth |first1=K. Then they drag the carcass into cover, occasionally over several hundred metres, to consume it. The nature of the tiger's hunting method and prey availability results in a "feast or famine" feeding style: they often consume {{Cvt|18|-|40|kg}} of meat at one time.<ref name=Mazak1981 /> In one study, tigresses from [[Nepal]] made about 40–50 kills a year and ate a minimum of {{cvt|5|-|6.3|kg}} of meat a day. Two males made about 40–50 kills in a year and ate {{cvt|6.3|-|7.8|kg}} of meat a day at the least.  <ref>Melvin E. Sunquest. [https://repository.si.edu/bitstream/handle/10088/6316/SCtZ-0336-Lo_res.pdf?sequence=2&isAllowed=y The Social Organization of Tigers (panthera tigris) in Royal Chitawan National Park, Nepal]. Smithsonian contributions to zoology. No.336</ref>

If injured, old or weak, or when its regular prey species become scarce, tigers often attack humans and become [[man-eater]]s.<ref name="mazak1996">{{Cite book |author=Mazak, V. |year=1996 |title=Der Tiger : ''Panthera tigris'' |location=Magdeburg, Heidelberg, Berlin, Oxford |publisher=Westarp Wissenschaften |isbn=978-3-89432-759-0}}</ref>

===Reproduction and lifecycle===
[[File:Bengal tigers, Karnataka, India.jpg|thumb|A male and female interact with each other in [[Karnataka]]]]
The tiger in India has no definite mating and birth seasons. Most young are born in December and April.<ref name="Brander1923" /> Young have also been found in March, May, October and November.<ref>{{Cite book |author=Sanderson, G. P. |year=1912 |url=https://archive.org/details/thirteenyearsamosf00sand |title=Thirteen years among the wild beasts of India: their haunts and habits from personal observations; with an account of the modes of capturing and taming elephants |publisher=John Grant |location=Edinburgh}}</ref> In the 1960s, certain aspects of tiger behaviour at [[Kanha National Park]] indicated that the peak of sexual activity was from November to about February, with some mating probably occurring throughout the year.<ref name=schaller1967>{{Cite book |author=Schaller, G. |year=1967 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KOVGHXfod0wC |title=The Deer and the Tiger: A Study of Wildlife in India |publisher=Chicago University Press |location=Chicago |isbn=9780226736570}}</ref>

Males reach maturity at 4–5 years of age, and females at 3–4 years. A Bengal comes into heat at intervals of about 3–9 weeks, and is receptive for 3–6 days. After a gestation period of 104–106 days, 1–4 cubs are born in a shelter situated in tall grass, thick bush or in caves. Newborn cubs weigh {{Cvt|780|to|1600|g|lb}} and they have a thick woolly fur that is shed after 3.5–5 months. Their eyes and ears are closed. Their milk teeth start to erupt at about 2–3 weeks after birth, and are slowly replaced by permanent dentition from 8.5 to 9.5 weeks of age onwards. They suckle for 3–6 months, and begin to eat small amounts of solid food at about 2 months of age. At this time, they follow their mother on her hunting expeditions and begin to take part in hunting at 5–6 months of age. At the age of 2–3 years, they slowly start to separate from the family group and become transient, looking out for an area, where they can establish their own home range. Young males move farther away from their native home range than young females. Once the family group has split, the mother comes into heat again.<ref name=Mazak1981 />

==Threats==
None of the ''Tiger Conservation Landscapes'' within the Bengal tiger range is large enough to support an effective population size of 250 individuals. Habitat losses and the extremely large-scale incidences of [[poaching]] are serious threats to the species' survival.<ref name=iucn/>

The [[Forest Rights Act]] passed by the Indian government in 2006 grants some of India's most impoverished communities the right to own and live in the forests, which likely brings them into conflict with wildlife and under-resourced, under-trained, ill-equipped forest department staff. In the past, evidence showed that humans and tigers cannot co-exist.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Buncombe |first=A. |date=31 October 2007 |title=The face of a doomed species |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/environment/nature/the-face-of-a-doomed-species-398373.html |newspaper=The Independent}}</ref>

===Poaching===
The most significant immediate threat to the existence of wild tiger populations is the [[Wildlife trade#Illegal wildlife trade|illegal wildlife trade]] in poached skins and body parts between India, Nepal and China. The governments of these countries have failed to implement adequate enforcement response, and wildlife crime remained a low priority in terms of political commitment and investment for years. There are well-organised gangs of professional poachers, who move from place to place and set up camp in vulnerable areas. Skins are rough-cured in the field and handed over to dealers, who send them for further treatment to Indian [[Tanning (leather)|tanning]] centres. Buyers choose the skins from dealers or tanneries and smuggle them through a complex interlinking network to markets outside India, mainly in China. Other factors contributing to their loss are [[urbanisation]] and revenge killing. Farmers blame tigers for killing cattle and shoot them. Their skins and body parts may however become a part of the illegal trade.<ref name="eia2006">{{Cite report |author=Banks, D. |name-list-style=amp |author2=Lawson, S. |author3=Wright, B. |year=2006 |title=Skinning the Cat: Crime and Politics of the Big Cat Skin Trade |location=London |publisher=Environmental Investigation Agency, Wildlife Protection Society of India |url=http://www.wpsi-india.org/images/EIA-WPSI_Skinning_The_Cat.pdf}}</ref> In Bangladesh, tigers are killed by professional poachers, local hunters, trappers, pirates and villagers. Each group of people has different motives for killing tigers, ranging from profit, excitement to safety concerns. All groups have access to the illegal wildlife trade in body parts.<ref>{{Cite journal |author1=Saif, S. |author2=Rahman, H. M. T. |author3=MacMillan, D. C. |name-list-style=amp |year=2016 |title=Who is killing the tiger ''Panthera tigris'' and why? |journal=Oryx |volume=52|pages=1–9 |doi=10.1017/S0030605316000491 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |author1=Saif, S. |author2=Russell, A. M. |author3=Nodie, S. I. |author4=Inskip, C. |author5=Lahann, P. |author6=Barlow, A. |author7=Barlow Greenwood, C. |author8=Islam, M. A. |author9=MacMillan, D. C. |name-list-style=amp |year=2016 |title=Local usage of Tiger parts and its role in Tiger killing in the Bangladesh Sundarbans |journal=Human Dimensions of Wildlife |volume=21 |issue=2 |pages=95–110 |doi=10.1080/10871209.2015.1107786 |s2cid=147189479}}</ref>

The illicit demand for bones and body parts from wild tigers for use in [[Traditional Chinese medicine#Animal substances|Traditional Chinese medicine]] is the reason for the unrelenting poaching pressure on tigers on the Indian subcontinent. ===Human–tiger conflict===
{{Main|Tiger attack}}
The Indian subcontinent has served as a stage for intense confrontations between tigers and people. At the beginning of the 19th century tigers were so numerous, that the killing of tigers was officially rewarded in many localities. The Terai region supported large numbers of tigers that were pushed into marginal habitat after the 1950s, when the conversion of natural habitat for paddy fields increased. Marauding tigers began to take a toll of human life in areas bordering cultivation. They are thought to have followed domestic livestock that wintered in the plains when they returned to the hills in the spring, and then being left without prey when the herds dispersed back to their respective villages. These tigers were the old, the young and the disabled. All suffered from some disability, mainly caused either by gunshot wounds or [[porcupine]] quills.<ref name=mcdougal1987>{{Cite book |last=McDougal |first=C. |date=1987 |chapter=The man-eating tigers in geographical historical perspective |editor-last1=Tilson |editor-first=R. L. |editor-last2=Seal |editor-first2=U. S. |title=Tigers of the World: The Biology, Biopolitics, Management, and Conservation of an Endangered Species |location=New Jersey |publisher=Noyes Publications |pages=435–448 |isbn=978-0-8155-1133-5}}</ref>

In the Sundarbans, 10 out of 13-man-eaters recorded in the 1970s were males, and they accounted for 86% of the victims. These man-eaters have been grouped into the ''confirmed'' or dedicated ones who go hunting especially for human prey; and the ''opportunistic'' ones, who do not search for humans but will, if they encounter a man, attack, kill and devour him. In areas where opportunistic man-eaters were found, the killing of humans was correlated with their availability, most victims being claimed during the [[honey]]-gathering season.<ref>{{Cite journal|author=Hendrichs, H. |year=1975|title=The status of the tiger (''Panthera tigris'') in the Sundarbans Mangrove|journal= Säugetierkundliche Mitteilungen |volume=23 |pages=161–199}}</ref> Tigers in the Sunderbans presumably attacked humans who entered their territories in search of wood, honey or fish, thus causing them to defend their territories. The number of tiger attacks on humans may be higher outside suitable areas for tigers, where numerous people are present, but with little wild prey for tigers.<ref>{{Cite journal |author=Jackson, P. |year=1985|title=Man-eaters |journal=International Wildlife |volume=15 |pages=4–11}}</ref>

In Nepal, the incidence of man-eating tigers has been only sporadic. In Chitwan National Park no cases were recorded before 1980. In the following few years, 13 people have been killed and eaten in the park and its environs. In the majority of cases, man-eating appeared to have been related to an intra-specific competition among male tigers.<ref name=mcdougal1987 />
An interview survey with 499 local people in Chitwan revealed that lower caste Hindus and people with less than eight years of formal education had negative attitudes to the tiger; most of them owned livestock and had heard about tigers attacking people and livestock.<ref>{{Cite journal |author1=Carter, N.H. |author2=Riley, S.J. |author3=Shortridge, A. |author4=Shrestha, B.K. |author5=Liu, J. |date=2014 |title=Spatial assessment of attitudes toward Tigers in Nepal |journal=Ambio |volume=43 |issue=2 |pages=125–137 |doi=10.1007/s13280-013-0421-7 |pmc=3906475 |pmid=23836312}}</ref>

In December 2012, a tiger was shot by the [[Kerala Forest Department]] on a [[coffee plantation]] on the fringes of the [[Wayanad Wildlife Sanctuary]]. Chief Wildlife Warden of Kerala ordered the hunt for the animal after mass protests erupted as the tiger had been carrying away livestock. The Forest Department had constituted a special task force to capture the animal with the assistance of a 10-member Special Tiger Protection Force and two trained [[Indian elephant]]s from the [[Bandipur Tiger Reserve]] in [[Karnataka]].<ref>{{Cite news |title=Straying tiger meets with a bloody end |url=http://www.thehindu.com/news/national/kerala/straying-tiger-meets-with-a-bloody-end/article4159420.ece |newspaper=The Hindu |date=3 December 2012}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Manoj |first=E. M. |date=3 December 2012|title=Tiger gone, but tension simmers |url=http://www.thehindu.com/news/national/kerala/tiger-gone-but-tension-simmers/article4159442.ece |newspaper=The Hindu}}</ref>

==Conservation efforts==
{{Main|Tiger conservation}}
An area of special interest lies in the "Terai Arc Landscape" in the [[Himalaya]]n foothills of northern India and southern Nepal, where 11 [[protected area]]s composed of dry forest foothills and tall-grass savannas harbour tigers in a {{Convert|49000|km2|mi2}} landscape. The goals are to manage tigers as a single [[metapopulation]], the dispersal of which between core refuges can help maintain genetic, demographic, and ecological integrity, and to ensure that species and [[habitat conservation]] becomes mainstreamed into the rural development agenda. In Nepal a community-based tourism model has been developed with a strong emphasis on sharing benefits with local people and on the regeneration of degraded forests. The approach has been successful in reducing poaching, restoring habitats, and creating a local constituency for conservation.<ref name="future">Damania, R., Seidensticker, J., Whitten, T., Sethi, G., Mackinnon, K., Kiss, A., Kushlin, A. (2008). [http://si-pddr.si.edu/dspace/bitstream/10088/7930/1/986D8887-2F38-44FE-96A2-A59C8FAE96BE.pdf ''A Future for Wild Tigers'']. World Bank, Washington, D.C. {{ISBN|0-8213-6792-7}}</ref>

[[World Wide Fund for Nature|WWF]] partnered with [[Leonardo DiCaprio]] to form a global campaign, "Save Tigers Now", with the ambitious goal of building political, financial and public support to double the wild tiger population by 2022.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.savetigersnow.org/solutions|title=WWF and leonardo partner to protect Tiger Habitat through Save Tigers Now|access-date=30 October 2012|publisher=SaveTigersNow.org|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121130014219/http://www.savetigersnow.org/solutions|archive-date=30 November 2012}}</ref> ''Save Tigers Now'' started its campaign in 12 different WWF Tiger priority landscapes, since May 2010.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://worldwildlife.org/press_releases/world-wildlife-fund-announces-partnership-with-leonardo-dicaprio-to-save-tigers-now|year=2010|title=Global Tiger Conservation initiative kick started Conservation Campaign in 2010|access-date=30 October 2012|publisher=World Wild Fund|archive-date=19 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210419160257/https://www.worldwildlife.org/press-releases/world-wildlife-fund-announces-partnership-with-leonardo-dicaprio-to-save-tigers-now|url-status=dead}}</ref>

This population of tigers has been assessed at the local level in several countries. It is listed as [[Endangered]] in Nepal,<ref>{{cite book |author1=Jnawali, S.R. |author2=Baral, H.S. |author3=Lee, S. |author4=Acharya, K.P. |author5=Upadhyay, G.P. |author6=Pandey, M. |author7=Shrestha, R. |author8=Joshi, D. |author9=Laminchhane, B.R. |author10=Griffiths, J. |author11=Khatiwada, A.P. |author12=Subedi, N. |author13=Amin, R. |year=2011 |title=The Status of Nepal Mammals |series=The National Red List Series |publisher=Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation |location=Kathmandu, Nepal |name-list-style=amp |isbn=9780900881602 |chapter=''Panthera tigris'' (Mazak, 1968), Subspecies ''Panthera tigris tigris'' (Linnaeus, 1758) |pages=73–74 |url=https://awsassets.panda.org/downloads/nepal_redlist_low_09_06_2012_1.pdf}}</ref> India,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://faunaofindia.nic.in/PDFVolumes/spb/023/index.pdf|title=Fauna of India}}</ref> and Bhutan,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://bt.chm-cbd.net/sites/bt/files/inline-files/Biodiversity%20Userlist_0.pdf|title=Biodiversity of Bhutan|website=bt.chm-cbd.net}}</ref> While Bangladesh<ref>{{cite web|url=https://portals.iucn.org/library/sites/library/files/documents/RL-549.3-003-v.2.pdf|title=Red List Of Bangladesh|website=portals.iucn.org}}</ref> and China<ref>{{cite journal |title=Red List of China's Vertebrates |date=2016 |journal=Biodiversity Science |volume=24 |issue=5 |pages=500–551 |author1=Jiang, Z. |author2=Jiang, J. |author3=Wang, Y. |author4=Zhang, E. |doi=10.17520/biods.2016076 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/304016077}}</ref> list it as [[Critically Endangered]].

===In India===
{{Main|Project Tiger}}
[[File:Great Indian Tiger 3 at Indira Gandhi Zoological Park, Visakhapatnam.jpg|thumb| Tigers at [[Indira Gandhi Zoological Park]], [[Visakhapatnam]], [[Andhra Pradesh]]]]

In 1973, [[Project Tiger]] was launched aiming at ensuring a viable tiger population in the country and preserving areas of biological importance as a natural heritage for the people. The project's task force visualised these [[Tiger reserves in India|tiger reserves]] as breeding nuclei, from which surplus animals would disperse to adjacent forests. The selection of areas for the reserves represented as close as possible the diversity of [[ecosystem]]s across the tiger's distribution in the country. Funds and commitment were mustered to support the intensive program of habitat protection and rehabilitation under the project. By the late 1980s, the initial nine reserves covering an area of {{Convert|9115|km2|sqmi}} had been increased to 15 reserves covering an area of {{Convert|24700|km2|sqmi}}. More than 1100 tigers were estimated to inhabit the reserves by 1984.<ref>Panwar, H. S. (1987). [https://books.google.com/books?id=YdC-wfyZwZEC&lpg=PP1&pg=PA110 "Project Tiger: The reserves, the tigers, and their future"]. In: Tilson, R. L., Seal, U. S., Minnesota Zoological Garden, IUCN/SSC Captive Breeding Group, IUCN/SSC Cat Specialist Group. ''Tigers of the world: the biology, biopolitics, management, and conservation of an endangered species''. Noyes Publications, Park Ridge, N.J., pp. 110–117, {{ISBN|0815511337}}.</ref><ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20140822212341/http://projecttiger.nic.in/content/107_1_Background.aspx Background]. National Tiger Conservation Authority, Government of India</ref>

Through this initiative the population decline was reversed initially, but has resumed in recent years; India's tiger population decreased from 3,642 in the 1990s to just over 1,400 from 2002 to 2008.<ref>Ramesh, R. (2008). [https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2008/feb/13/endangeredspecies.india?gusrc=rss&feed=environment "Indian wild tiger numbers almost halve"]. ''Guardian News and Media Limited''.</ref>

The Indian [[Wildlife Protection Act of 1972]] enables government agencies to take strict measures so as to ensure the conservation of the Bengal tigers. The [[Wildlife Institute of India]] estimates showed that tiger numbers had fallen in [[Madhya Pradesh]] by 61%, [[Maharashtra]] by 57%, and [[Rajasthan]] by 40%. The government's first tiger census, conducted under the Project Tiger initiative begun in 1973, counted 1,827 tigers in the country that year. Using that methodology, the government observed a steady population increase, reaching 3,700 tigers in 2002. However, the use of more reliable and independent censusing technology including [[camera trap]]s for the 2007–2008 all-India census has shown that the numbers were in fact less than half than originally claimed by the Forest Department.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Just 1,411 tigers in India |author=Sethi, N. |url=http://articles.timesofindia.indiatimes.com/2008-02-13/flora-fauna/27773614_1_tiger-population-sariska-tiger-numbers |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110811044737/http://articles.timesofindia.indiatimes.com/2008-02-13/flora-fauna/27773614_1_tiger-population-sariska-tiger-numbers |url-status=dead |archive-date=11 August 2011 |year=2008 |work=[[The Times of India]] | access-date=3 March 2009}}</ref>

===In Bangladesh===
WildTeam is working with local communities and the Bangladesh Forest Department to reduce human-tiger conflict in the Bangladesh Sundarbans. For over 100 years people, tigers, and livestock have been injured and killed in the conflict; in recent decades up to 50 people, 80 livestock, and 3 tigers have been killed in a year. Now, through WildTeam's work, there is a boat-based Tiger Response team that provides first aid, transport, and body retrieval support for people being killed in the forest by tigers. WildTeam has also set up 49 volunteer Village Response Teams that are trained to save tigers that have strayed into the village areas and would be otherwise killed. These village teams are made up of over 350 volunteers, who are also now supporting anti-poaching work and conservation education/awareness activities. WildTeam also works to empower local communities to access the government funds for compensating the loss/injury of livestock and people from the conflict. To monitor the conflict and assess the effectiveness of actions, WildTeam have also set up a human-tiger conflict data collection and reporting system.

==="Re-wilding" project in South Africa===
In 2000, the Bengal tiger re-wilding project ''Tiger Canyons'' was started by [[John Varty]], who together with the zoologist [[Dave Salmoni]] trained captive-bred tiger cubs how to stalk, hunt, associate hunting with food and regain their predatory instincts. They claimed that once the tigers proved that they can sustain themselves in the wild, they would be released into a free-range sanctuary of [[South Africa]] to fend for themselves.<ref>{{Cite web |year=2001 |title=Meet the Tiger Men: John Varty |url=http://dsc.discovery.com/convergence/tigers/trainers/trainers_02.html |website=Discovery Channel |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080603034011/http://dsc.discovery.com/convergence/tigers/trainers/trainers_02.html |archive-date=3 June 2008}}</ref>

The project has received controversy after accusations by their investors and conservationists of manipulating the behaviour of the tigers for the purpose of a film production, ''[[Living with Tigers]]'', with the tigers believed to be unable to hunt.<ref name="envirolink">{{Cite web |title=Tiger Film a Fraud, says The Chinese Tigers South African Trust |url=http://lists.envirolink.org/pipermail/ar-news/Week-of-Mon-20030901/005990.html |date=2003 |agency=PR Newswire |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110727084010/http://lists.envirolink.org/pipermail/ar-news/Week-of-Mon-20030901/005990.html |archive-date=27 July 2011 }}</ref><ref name="wildeye">{{Cite web|title=Discovery Film Proclaimed A Fraud; Broadcaster to be Sued |url=http://www.wildeye.co.uk/wildlife-film/Wfn/wfn56.htm |website=Wildlife Film News 56 |date=February 2004 |access-date=27 August 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090607012741/http://www.wildeye.co.uk/wildlife-film/Wfn/wfn56.htm |archive-date=7 June 2009}}</ref> Stuart Bray, who had originally invested a large sum of money in the project, claimed that he and his wife, Li Quan, watched the film crew "[chase] the prey up against the fence and into the path of the tigers just for the sake of dramatic footage."<ref name="envirolink" /><ref name="wildeye" />

The four tigers involved in this project have been confirmed to be crossbred Siberian–Bengal tigers, which should neither be used for breeding nor being released into the [[Karoo]]. Tigers that are not genetically pure will not be able to participate in the tiger [[Species Survival Plan]], as they are not used for breeding, and are not allowed to be released into the wild.<ref name="arrick2007">{{Cite web |author1=Arrick, A. |author2= Mckinney, K. |date=2007 |url=http://www.tylerpaper.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=/20070813/NEWS01/708130305 |title=Purrrfect Breed? |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090111090603/http://www.tylerpaper.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=%2F20070813%2FNEWS01%2F708130305 |archive-date=11 January 2009 |work=TylerPaper |url-status=dead}}</ref>

The tiger is one of the animals displayed on the [[Pashupati seal]] of the [[Indus Valley civilisation]]. The tiger crest is the emblem on the [[Chola dynasty|Chola]] coins. The seals of several Chola copper coins show the tiger, the [[Pandyan Dynasty|Pandya]] emblem fish and the [[Chera Dynasty|Chera]] emblem bow, indicating that the Cholas had achieved political supremacy over the latter two dynasties. Gold coins found in Kavilayadavalli in the [[Nellore district]] of [[Andhra Pradesh]] have motifs of the tiger, bow and some indistinct marks.<ref>{{Cite book |author=Singh, U. |year=2008 |title=A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India: From the Stone Age to the 12th Century |location=India |publisher=Pearson Education |pages=51–57 |chapter=Numismatics: the study of coins |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=H3lUIIYxWkEC&pg=PA54 |isbn=978-8131711200}}</ref>

Today, the tiger is the [[List of national animals|national animal]] of Bangladesh and India. Bangladeshi banknotes feature a tiger. The political party [[Muslim League (Pakistan)|Muslim League]] of Pakistan uses the tiger as its election symbol.<ref name="Jackson1999">{{Cite book |last=Jackson |first=P. |date=1999 |chapter=The tiger in human consciousness and its significance in crafting solutions for tiger conservation |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dbQ8AAAAIAAJ&pg=PA50 |editor1-last=Seidensticker |editor1-first=J. |editor2-last=Christie |editor2-first=S. |editor3-last=Jackson |editor3-first=P. |title=Riding the Tiger: Tiger Conservation in Human-Dominated Landscapes |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |pages=50–54 |isbn=978-0-521-64835-6}}</ref>
[[Tipu Sultan]], who ruled [[Kingdom of Mysore|Mysore]] in late 18th-century India, was also a great admirer of the animal. The famed 18th-century [[automaton]], [[Tipu's Tiger]] was also created for him.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Brittlebank |first=K. |date=May 1995 |title=Sakti and Barakat: The Power of Tipu's Tiger. An Examination of the Tiger Emblem of Tipu Sultan of Mysore |journal=Modern Asian Studies |volume=29 |issue=2 |pages=257–269 |doi=10.1017/S0026749X00012725 |jstor=312813|s2cid=145790819 }}</ref> The tiger was the dynastic symbol of this dynasty.<ref name=Sramek2006>{{Cite journal |last1=Sramek |first1=J. |date=2006 |title='Face Him Like a Briton': Tiger Hunting, Imperialism, and British Masculinity in Colonial India, 1800–1875 |journal=Victorian Studies |volume=48 |issue=4 |pages=659–680 <!-- |doi=10.1353/vic.2007.0035 broken --> |doi=10.2979/vic.2006.48.4.659 |jstor=4618910|s2cid=145632352 }}</ref>
The iconography persisted and during the [[Indian Rebellion of 1857]], [[Punch (magazine)|Punch]] ran a political cartoon showing the Indian rebels as a tiger, attacking a victim, being defeated by the British forces shown by the larger figure of a lion.<ref name="Carter_1893_Medals">{{Cite book |location=London |title=War medals of the British army, and how they were won |url=https://archive.org/details/warmedalsofbriti00cartrich |last=Carter |first=T. |author-link=Thomas Carter (writer) |edition=Revised, enlarged <!--|publisher=Norie and Wilson -->|publisher=W. H. Long |year=1893 |ol=14047956M}}</ref>

Several people were nicknamed Tiger or Bengal Tiger. Bengali revolutionary Jatindranath Mukherjee was called [[Bagha Jatin]] ([[Bengali language|Bengali]] for Tiger Jatin). Educator [[Sir Ashutosh Mukherjee]] was often called the "Tiger of Bengal".

The Bengal tiger has been used as a logo and a nickname for famous personalities. Some of them are mentioned below:
* Members of the [[East Bengal Regiment]] of the [[Bangladesh Army]] are nicked 'Bengal Tigers'; the regiment's logo is a tiger face. [[Senior Tigers]] is the nickname of the first battalion.
* The German [[King Tiger]] heavy tank was named for the Bengal Tiger.
* [[Bangladesh National Cricket Team]] bears the nickname "The Tigers".
